summaries.example: Imagine the true answer is that there are 8 planets. Saying there are 9 planets is wrong, but it is much closer than saying there are 9 billion. A claim can be wrong yet still be a useful step toward the truth.
summaries.summary: Truthlikeness is the idea that beliefs can be compared by how close they are to the truth. This is helpful because many scientific ideas are later changed or replaced, yet they may still contain useful pieces of truth. For example, saying that there are 9 planets is false, but it is closer to the truth than saying there are 9 billion. Philosophers study how to compare such claims. Some focus on the true and false information in a claim. Some focus on its important results or consequences. Others imagine possible ways the world could be and compare how similar those possibilities are to the real world. Each method has difficulties. A method might count too many unhelpful details, depend too much on the words used, or give surprising rankings. The larger question is whether inquiry can make progress even when people do not possess the whole truth.
key_ideas: A claim is not only true or false; some claims can be closer to the truth than others.
A false idea about 9 planets is closer to the truth than a false idea about 9 billion planets.
A true statement can also be incomplete. Saying there are at least 0 planets is true, but it tells us less than saying there are between 7 and 9.
Philosophers have proposed different ways to measure closeness to truth, and no single approach has won general agreement.
summaries.why_it_matters: Truthlikeness helps explain how learning and science might improve without being perfect. It gives us a way to talk about useful mistakes, incomplete answers, and theories that are later corrected. It also reminds us that being certain is different from making progress. Philosophers still disagree about the best way to measure closeness to truth.

important_terms.definition: Truth: what is actually the case about something.
Truthlikeness: how close a claim seems to the complete truth, even when the claim is not completely correct.
Inquiry: a careful search for answers or knowledge.
Fallibilism: the idea that people and scientists can be mistaken, even when they are trying carefully to learn.

questions_to_think_about: Can a wrong answer still help someone learn?
Which is more useful: a very general true statement or a nearly correct statement?
How could we tell whether a new scientific idea is getting closer to the truth?
Does knowing one true fact always improve what we believe overall?

summaries.example: Suppose the actual number of planets is 8. The claim N=9 is false but intuitively closer to the truth than N=9 billion. Yet a true claim such as N≥0 is less informative than 7≤N≤9. A more striking case is that the false claim N=9 may seem closer to the complete truth than the true claim N≠9, because the latter leaves many possibilities open. These comparisons show why truthlikeness cannot be reduced simply to truth value.
summaries.summary: Truthlikeness is a proposed ordering of propositions that is finer-grained than the true/false distinction. The motivation is straightforward: inquiry may aim at truth while proceeding through theories that are incomplete or even strictly false. The logical problem is to define this ordering without producing unacceptable results. The content approach compares truth content and falsity content, but Popper-inspired versions lead to theorems making falsehoods uniformly inferior or produce the implausible result that adding arbitrary content improves false theories. The consequence approach restricts attention to relevant consequences, yet relevance is difficult to specify and may depend on the expressive framework. The likeness approach instead assigns similarity or distance relations to possible worlds and seeks a rule for extending those relations to sets of worlds represented by propositions. This creates an extension problem: even a fixed world-distance function may support several incompatible measures of propositional distance. It also raises framework dependence, since alternative primitive descriptions can reverse apparent similarity judgments. Beyond the logical problem, the epistemological problem asks whether truthlikeness can be estimated from evidence when the truth is unknown. Expected truthlikeness offers one such estimate, but it depends on both a truthlikeness measure and rational credences over possible truths. The axiological problem concerns cognitive value: whether accurate or truthlike belief is valuable in its own right, and how to measure that value. The entry concludes that there is still no broadly accepted solution combining all these demands.
key_ideas: Truthlikeness is motivated by the combination of realism, optimism about inquiry, and fallibilism: inquiry aims at truth, progress is possible, but theories may be false.
The content approach faces problems because counting true and false consequences can trivialize comparisons, while content alone cannot distinguish many different ways of being false.
The consequence approach tries to count only relevant consequences, but it must explain relevance, extend beyond simple examples, and address language dependence.
The likeness approach models possible worlds and their distances from the actual world. It then faces an extension problem: there may be many ways to turn world-distance into proposition-distance.
Truthlikeness is not the same as probability. A highly informative claim can be unlikely while still being closer to the truth than a safe but uninformative claim.
The epistemological and axiological problems remain after the logical problem: how can we estimate truthlikeness from evidence, and what cognitive value should truth or approximation to truth have?
summaries.why_it_matters: Truthlikeness addresses a central tension in the philosophy of science. Scientific realism treats truth as the aim of inquiry, while fallibilism recognizes that accepted theories can be false and later replaced. A satisfactory account would explain how rational progress is possible without claiming infallibility. The issue also affects how we assess evidence, theory change, belief revision, and the cognitive value of learning. The source emphasizes that the main approaches each capture some intuitive judgments but also face serious unresolved difficulties.

important_terms.definition: Truthlikeness, also called verisimilitude, is a comparative property intended to rank propositions by their closeness to the complete truth.
Logical problem: the task of giving a consistent, materially adequate account of truthlikeness and its ordering properties.
Content approach: an approach that compares how much true and false information a theory contains or entails.
Consequence approach: an approach that compares theories through selected consequences, with relevant true consequences supporting and relevant false consequences opposing truthlikeness.
Likeness approach: a semantic approach that compares possibilities or worlds by their similarity to the actual world, then extends that comparison to propositions.
Framework dependence: the worry that judgments of similarity and truthlikeness can change when an equivalent subject matter is described using different basic concepts.
Expected truthlikeness: an evidence-based estimate of a proposition's objective truthlikeness, weighted by how credible the possible complete truths are.

questions_to_think_about: Should a theory receive credit for every true consequence it entails, or only for relevant ones?
Can a false but highly informative theory be closer to the truth than a weak true statement?
If two descriptions use different basic predicates but express the same possibilities, should their truthlikeness rankings agree?
Does learning a true fact necessarily make a whole belief system more truthlike?
Can a measure of cognitive accuracy both respect closeness to truth and avoid recommending belief revision without new evidence?

summaries.example: Suppose a class is trying to discover how many planets are in the solar system, and the correct answer is 8. The answer 9 is false but fairly close. The answer 9 billion is also false, but much farther away. Meanwhile, “there are at least 0 planets” is true but not very informative. This suggests that truth and falsehood alone do not tell us enough about how good a claim is.
summaries.summary: Truthlikeness is a philosophical idea for comparing claims that are not equally close to the truth. A simple true/false division cannot capture all the differences that matter in inquiry. For example, a claim that there are 9 planets is false if the correct number is 8, but it is closer than a claim about 9 billion. A true claim can also be incomplete and less informative than another true claim. The entry describes three broad approaches to the logical problem. The content approach compares the amount of true and false information in a theory. The consequence approach compares theories by their consequences, while trying to count only consequences that are relevant rather than every logical result. The likeness approach compares possible worlds with the actual world and uses their similarity to estimate how close a proposition is to the truth. Each approach has objections. Content measures can reward arbitrary additions to false theories. Consequence measures need a convincing account of relevance. Likeness measures must explain both how worlds are similar and how similarities among worlds produce a ranking of propositions. They may also depend on the framework or vocabulary used to describe possibilities. The entry then distinguishes truthlikeness from probability and discusses two further questions: whether evidence gives us access to degrees of truthlikeness, and whether truthlike belief has cognitive value.
key_ideas: Truthlikeness is meant to explain why some false scientific theories can still represent progress.
The content approach compares the true and false information supported by theories. Its critics argue that simply adding information can make a false theory look better for the wrong reason.
The consequence approach counts consequences, but it must decide which consequences are relevant. Counting every consequence can double-count information and create bad results.

The likeness approach compares possible worlds with the actual world, then asks how close a whole proposition is to the truth. It must decide how to combine the distances of all the worlds represented by that proposition.
Truthlikeness is different from probability. A claim may be unlikely but informative and close to the truth; a claim may be probable because it says very little.
The source also asks whether we can recognize progress from evidence and whether truth or truthlikeness has special intellectual value.
summaries.why_it_matters: The idea matters because it offers a possible explanation of scientific progress that does not require perfect certainty. A theory can be mistaken yet improve on an earlier theory by getting more of the structure or details right. At the same time, truthlikeness warns us not to call every new claim progress: a change may add information while also adding serious errors. Studying the concept helps clarify how theories, evidence, uncertainty, and intellectual progress fit together.

important_terms.definition: Truthlikeness means being more or less close to the truth, rather than simply being true or false.
A proposition is a statement that can be evaluated as true or false.
Content is the information a claim provides, including what follows from it.
A consequence is a statement that follows logically from another statement or theory.
A possible world is a complete way things could be, used to compare alternatives with the actual world.
Framework dependence is the concern that closeness judgments may change when the same subject is described with different basic ideas or vocabulary.

questions_to_think_about: Why might a true but vague statement be less truthlike than a nearly correct false statement?
What should count as a relevant consequence of a theory?
If two descriptions use different basic concepts, should they always give the same closeness ranking?
Can scientists estimate progress without knowing the complete truth?
Is learning valuable even when it does not change what practical action we should take?
